Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes. ## Focus and continuity Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer. Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button. There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work. ## A useful review path The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`. These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible. For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update. --- open-forge: description: Label associations, responsive field rows, text editing surfaces and load-notice layout. tags: - Forms - Layout - Controls --- # Form layout guide This page explains the label, field and action arrangements used by the current controls. The game has two kinds of control groups: the always-visible deal bar and the text tools inside Reproduce a game. They share native elements and the `.control` style, but their DOM and layout differ. This guide describes those differences so a markup refactor can preserve the actual interaction rather than just one screenshot. ## A map of the current groups | Group | Markup and layout | Source | | --- | --- | --- | | Grid size | Label and select in a flex row | `Controls.tsx`, `controls.css` | | Deal actions | Two buttons in the outer wrapped flex row | `Controls.tsx` | | Board code | Form with label above a field/action row | `BoardCodeForm.tsx`, `reproduction.css` | | Snapshot JSON | Label and textarea in the panel's body grid | `Reproduction.tsx` | | Snapshot actions | Two buttons in a wrapped flex row | `Reproduction.tsx` | | Load outcome | Paragraph and conditional Resume in a wrapped row | `Reproduction.tsx` | Only Board code is wrapped in a form element. The snapshot field is controlled React state in Reproduction, and its buttons explicitly call callbacks. Enter in a multiline textarea remains text editing rather than submitting the snapshot. Enter in Board code invokes the form's submit path. ## Labels are visible and associated Grid size uses `htmlFor="grid-size"` and a select with that id. Board code uses `htmlFor="board-code"`, and Snapshot JSON uses `htmlFor="snapshot-json"`. The visible text supplies the fields' names; placeholders do not stand in for labels. Board code also has `name="boardCode"` because its form reads that field through FormData. Its id serves label association; its name serves native form data lookup. Those are different roles, and changing one does not automatically update the other. The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains the behavioral value of the current element choices. The labels come from `control-labels.ts`. Keeping visible text in those constants does not change the label/field relationship. A review can inspect both the imported value and the actual id association, because a correct label string next to the wrong id is still a broken field relationship. ## Deal bar: horizontal until it wraps The outer `.controls` container uses `display: flex`, bottom alignment, wrapping and a `12px` gap. The nested `.size-control` is a centered flex row with its own `12px` gap. On a wide layout, label, select and action buttons appear in one compact band above the statistics. At widths up to 599px, the outer container stretches its children. The size group takes the full line and distributes its label and select with space-between alignment. The direct child buttons grow equally. The DOM order stays Grid size, New Game, Restart while the layout moves into two lines. That stability matters for keyboard order. The CSS changes wrapping, not the tab sequence or source order. A visual rearrangement implemented by moving DOM nodes could affect where Tab goes; the present media query does not need to do that. The group is not a native form. Changing the select calls the controller immediately. There is no Apply button or submission that combines the selected size with one of the deal actions. [Control bar](control-bar.md) documents those callbacks and what they replace. ## Board-code form: one label, one submission BoardCodeForm renders a grid form with a `6px` gap. Its first child is the label. The next is `.control-row`, a wrapping flex container with a `12px` gap and bottom alignment. Inside are the input and the Load board submit button. The input has `flex: 1` and `width: 16ch`. The preferred width reflects code-like text, while flex growth gives it available space. The shared control stylesheet sets `min-width: 0` for inputs and textareas so their intrinsic width does not force the page wider than its container. The button is the form's explicit submit action. Its ref supports successful keyboard submission when the input is replaced. The form prevents normal page navigation, reads `boardCode` and calls the loader. The label stays outside the row so a wrapped button does not detach it from the field's visual group. On the phone breakpoint, direct child buttons of `.control-row` get `flex: 1`. This selector is shared with the snapshot action row. A wrapper inserted between the row and a button would change this rule's target; a DOM cleanup can therefore have a mobile layout consequence even when desktop placement looks unchanged. ## Snapshot field: a larger editing surface Reproduction's body is a grid with a `12px` gap and `4px 16px 16px` padding. The Snapshot JSON label and textarea are adjacent children of this grid. The textarea uses five rows, fills its available width and can resize vertically. Export replaces its value with readable JSON. Import reads the current value. There is no automatic serialization on every game render, so the field can hold a draft while the player inspects cards or changes a deal. Its controlled state is independent of the board-code input's generation-keyed default value. The two snapshot buttons follow in a `.control-row`. Both are `type="button"`, which makes the action semantics explicit even if the surrounding layout later changes. The current component does not depend on a textarea Enter press to decide which snapshot action to perform. A manual copy workflow uses native text selection. The card-specific `user-select: none` rule does not apply to this field. Vertical resize and long structured text can make the disclosure tall, but the field remains an ordinary part of document flow. ## Shared control styling `.control` sets minimum height, padding, border, radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. It is imported by both Controls and the reproduction components. The selectors for button and select add a pointer cursor, while the input and textarea selector handles shrinking. The shared class does not create a universal component with all semantics and validation built in. A select still has native options, an input still has its own maximum length, and a textarea still has multiline editing. Their association, callbacks and error descriptions remain in the JSX. `game.css` sets global border-box sizing and a system sans-serif font at `16px` with a `24px` line height. Form controls inherit the font instead of taking a separate browser default. The focus outline is shared through `:focus-visible`, so a form layout also needs enough space for that outline to be seen. ## Outcome text is outside the disclosure The load notice paragraph and Resume are in `.load-status`, following details rather than living inside `.reproduction-body`. The row has a `12px` gap, wraps and reserves at least `56px` of height. The paragraph grows and has `min-width: 0`. This placement makes a paused-load outcome usable after the disclosure closes. It also means a selector that searches only inside details will not find Resume or the notice. Tests deliberately inspect the adjacent load-status location. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows its content and the load buttons' `aria-describedby` relationships. Turn output is elsewhere, near the board instructions. The layout does not put every changing sentence inside the form body. The distinction is useful when testing a large phone board: result visibility near the board and load feedback near the text tools are separate observations. ## Reflow and review examples At a narrow width, the page should be read as a vertical flow of labeled groups rather than a fixed matrix of coordinates. The existing wrapped rows and shrinking fields let content determine height. The default board fits the narrow layout, while a large board confines its own overflow to its viewport. A longer draft can remain in an input even when not all of its characters are visible at once; native text editing can scroll within the field. That is different from making the whole outer page wider. A multiline snapshot can expand or scroll internally without turning its label into a floating overlay. The equivalent zoom test at `640x400`, device scale 2, checks readable controls, statistics and completion output. It also uses the snapshot tools at that constrained layout. `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` verifies labels, native limits and selectable export text. Together the sources cover geometry and editing behavior without defining a new generic form framework. For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) own its separate acceptance rules. The current interface has no name-field placeholder, character counter, error precedence or field order. --- open-forge: description: Active-time ownership, pause conditions, synchronization and logical interval handling. tags: - Architecture - Time - Session --- # Time policy This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions. There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch. ## Where observations enter `use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock. This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls. The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks. ## Conditions for active time The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won. A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action. An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval. Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation. ## Delta arithmetic `ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`. Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval. The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary. A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately. ## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe `CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta. This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation. When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds. ## Synchronize at action boundaries The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely. The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization. Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction. ## Mismatch time and elapsed time `advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`. A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time. The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play. The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events. ## Serialization has a rounding boundary Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects. The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback. The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) covers the visible statistic and limit. ## Deal generations and stale work Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path. The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes. Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model. ## Test evidence Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows those cases in detail, and [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runners. --- open-forge: description: Fresh seed selection, rejection sampling and the boundary with reproducible decks. tags: - Architecture - Randomness - Reproducibility --- # Randomness policy This page explains the boundary between choosing a fresh deal and reproducing a deal in Neon Pairs. A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. [Deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md) covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration. ## One boundary for fresh input `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game. The distinction is visible in the imports. `use-game.ts` imports `freshBoardCode` for fresh deals and `createGame` for constructing a game from a code. `game.ts` imports `generateBoard`, which works from supplied data. Nothing in a card component needs to choose a seed, and no deck is shuffled merely because React rendered it. ## Two finite ranges The fresh-board module uses a one-element `Uint32Array` and `crypto.getRandomValues`. Its possible raw values span the unsigned 32-bit range, with `UINT32_RANGE` set to `2 ** 32`. The allowed seed range is defined in `deck.ts` by `SEED_MAX = 2_147_483_646`. Valid codes use positive seeds, so the transformation adds one after taking a remainder. The module computes `RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX`. With the current values the limit is `4_294_967_292`. A draw below that limit is accepted; one at or above it is retried. Thus each allowed remainder has the same number of accepted raw values. The last four unsigned values do not enter the modulo mapping. The seed is `(draw % SEED_MAX) + 1`. Its endpoints are therefore 1 and `SEED_MAX`; zero is not produced. The code also checks that `buffer[0]` is defined, which matches the project's checked-index TypeScript setting even though the buffer length is deliberately one. It loops until it can return a valid code. This is rejection sampling, not rounding a floating-point draw. Applying a plain remainder to all `2 ** 32` possible values would assign a few seeds one more source value than the others. The difference is small numerically, but a reproducible format benefits from an implementation whose range treatment can be described exactly. ## Excluding the immediately previous seed When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change. That check is narrower than a history of every generated deal. The implementation does not keep a seed registry, does not persist a sequence of fresh codes and does not exclude every seed seen earlier in the session. A code can reappear after intervening games. Nor does the initial call pass an earlier browser session's seed; preferences retain size and best moves, not the last active deal. The retry loop also does not claim a bounded number of calls. It retries out-of-range draws and an excluded candidate. There is no time-based fallback in this module. A browser crypto failure is not caught here. The storage module's tolerant behavior should not be mistaken for a universal fallback around every browser API. ## Construction after selection Once the seed is selected, `boardCode(size, seed)` validates the representation. Its format is `np1-SIZE-SEED`, with the supported sizes supplied by `GRID_SIZES`. The parser accepts exactly the seven sizes 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. It also checks that the seed is a safe integer within the allowed maximum. `createGame(code)` calls `generateBoard(code)` and adds the initial progress fields. The starting deck is already determined by that point. The game starts with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed milliseconds and `started: false`. The code-producing function can throw for an invalid size or seed. The session's `newGame` action checks the requested size with `isValidSize` before requesting a fresh code. Its normal UI callers use the native select populated from `GRID_SIZES`. These checks protect the application path without adding a second size list to the form. ## Deterministic state is not ambient entropy `deck.ts` exports `nextRandomState(state)`, but this function is arithmetic over an explicit argument. It computes `(state * 16_807) % 2_147_483_647`. Repeating a call with the same state returns the same result. The name describes a pseudorandom sequence; it does not imply a browser read. For a valid seed, the generator advances that sequence inside a descending Fisher–Yates shuffle. The initial deck contains two copies of every integer face from zero to `size ** 2 / 2 - 1`, arranged as adjacent duplicates before shuffling. For a 4 by 4 board, it starts as `0, 0, 1, 1` and so on through face 7. At shuffle position `index`, the number of choices is `index + 1`. The implementation computes a divisible acceptance limit from `SEED_MAX`, advances its local generator state, subtracts one to form the draw, rejects values outside the limit and uses the accepted remainder as the swap position. Both the raw seed selection and the shuffle use rejection, but they operate on different ranges and have different owners. The maximum multiplication in the sequence is below JavaScript's safe integer limit. The independent browser-test oracle uses BigInt arithmetic, providing a separate expression of the same documented deal rather than calling the production generator to predict itself. [Purity guide](purity-guide.md) explains why explicit state makes these checks possible. ## A concrete stable example The fixture code `np1-4-1` produces this row-major deck: ```text 6 7 0 5 2 2 0 5 3 7 1 6 4 4 1 3 ``` Positions are zero based in rules and formats. Positions 2 and 6 are a pair; positions 0 and 11 are another. The fixture's `EXAMPLE_DECK` stores the whole literal sequence, while `EXAMPLE_PAIRS` lists the matching positions. Those are test facts, not attributes added to hidden cards in the shipped DOM. Changing the shuffle traversal, recurrence, rejection condition or starting deck would change this example and potentially every shared code. Such a change is therefore observable through board codes, snapshots and replays, even if the interface still looks like a memory game. The generator's determinism connects implementation detail to a public format. ## Every action that chooses or reuses a deal | Path | Seed behavior in the current implementation | | --- | --- | | Initial `useGame` state | Fresh seed using the saved valid size or default size | | New Game | Fresh seed excluding the current seed | | Grid-size selection | Fresh seed for the selected size, excluding the current seed | | Restart | Existing board code passed to `createGame` | | Load board | Submitted code trimmed, parsed and reconstructed | | Load snapshot | Decoder validates its code and reconstructs its deck | | Replay | Reader validates the supplied code and starts from it | This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards. `newGame` also resets the clock and replaces the session game. Seed choice alone does not clear progress or focus; session replacement and the generation key supply those lifetimes. [Session module](session-module.md) covers that process. ## Evidence and blind spots `deck.test.ts` covers board-code parsing, generated structure and known vectors. `deck-rejection.test.ts` reads independent BigInt vectors for an over-limit draw and a draw exactly on the shuffle limit. The equality boundary matters because accepting it would break the uniform mapping and alter the deterministic result for that seed. The browser suite loads documented codes through actual controls and uses `specDeal` from `tests/deal-oracle.ts` when it needs an independent deal. `lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` checks that New Game changes the current code and that a size change chooses a different seed from the previous deal. A complete all-size journey checks that the resulting decks remain playable. The fresh-board module has no adjacent unit test. Deterministic deck tests establish format behavior and known sequences, rather than statistical properties of the browser entropy source. The raw seed boundary is short enough to inspect directly, but inspection is a different kind of evidence. The source audit's core list rejects browser entropy references in the named core files. It does not implement a whole-program information-flow proof or a general scanner for every possible source of variation. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes precisely what it scans. ## Diagnosing an unexpected deck The most useful reproduction is the board code, not the time the game started. Parsing that code reveals both size and seed. Calling `generateBoard` with it establishes the expected deck without involving React or browser state. An imported snapshot reconstructs that same deck and then validates progress against it. If the code differs, investigate which action replaced the session. If the code agrees but the deck differs, compare the shuffle against the literal vector and independent oracle. If the deck agrees but the wrong art appears, investigate `faceDesign`, reveal state and card props. These are distinct failures with different evidence. A hidden card deliberately receives `null` as its face prop. Looking for all face identities in its DOM is not a valid debugging strategy for this application boundary. Tests already have the code and can derive a deck independently. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) describes that presentation decision in context. --- open-forge: description: Session fields, controller actions, replacement generations and preference effects. tags: - Architecture - Session - State --- # Session module This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences. The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence. ## The Session value `Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves. These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state. The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model. ## Initialization `initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences. The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot. `browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called. ## The current ref and React state `useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`. This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game. The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences. ## Card activation The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match. `activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet. For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn. A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus. ## Why feedback has an event counter Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events. A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice. `loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message. ## Replacing a game `replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices. If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation. A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves. The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime. ## Controller actions | Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game | | `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal | | `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice | | `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice | | `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text | | `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation | | `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback | The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically. The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact. ## Logical ticks `tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too. A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer. The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps. ## Preferences and effects `Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`. `rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect. `useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails. The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method. ## Focus is a neighboring concern The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session. ## Evidence and investigation `session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture. `storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface. For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

# ADR 058: Give additional stored data a distinct namespace

This record explains the naming rule for new stored data while preserving the existing preferences key.

## Context

The first storage decision used a game prefix, a data-family segment and a version suffix separated by dots. The current preferences key still demonstrates that choice: `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. It contains a selected size and a map of per-size best moves in a versioned JSON value.

Additional stored families need a recognizable naming convention without turning a documentation change into an unnecessary migration of existing preferences. This record supersedes [ADR 011](adr-011-storage-keys.md). The scope is key naming; it does not add another stored family to the current game or replace snapshot export with automatic progress saving.

## Decision

The namespace distinguishes newly introduced storage from keys that a released game already reads. New stored data uses a key of the form np3:THING, where THING is a lowercase plural noun for what is stored. Keys that already exist keep their names. This lets a reader recognize the new convention while the existing preference reader continues to find its current value.

The distinction is intentionally about whether a key already exists, rather than whether its contents look old. Renaming preferences merely to make the key look consistent would require a migration, conflict handling and evidence that the saved size and records survived. No such migration is implemented in the source.

## What remains unchanged in the implementation

`PREFERENCES_KEY` is the one existing key used by `readPreferences` and `writePreferences`. The stored JSON carries `schemaVersion: 1`, `size` and `bestMoves`. Naming a storage key and validating the value are separate responsibilities. A recognizable namespace cannot establish that JSON is well formed, that a size is supported or that a score is a plausible bounded integer.

The parser treats saved data as unknown, checks supported values and falls back to usable defaults when access or validation fails. Writes are caught so the in-memory game remains playable. The namespace decision does not move those browser effects into pure game functions. [Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [Storage failure policy](../persistence/storage-failure-policy.md) describe the existing behavior.

## Alternatives and tradeoffs

Renaming every key at once would make the storage inspector look uniform, but would create work and risk unrelated to the new naming need. Continuing the original dotted pattern indefinitely would avoid any new convention while leaving this replacement decision without effect. The selected approach separates continuity for existing data from a clear naming choice for additions.

A single giant application value could avoid choosing new keys at all. That would couple unrelated data families to the same read, validation and write path. The current preferences envelope is appropriately small for size and best moves.

## Reading the rule accurately

The namespace marker is not a new board-code prefix, snapshot version or replay version. Those public formats retain their own identifiers. It is also not a claim that the current preferences schema has been upgraded. Confusing these layers would create a format change where only storage-key naming was intended.

The current source provides a concrete compatibility check: a reader can inspect `PREFERENCES_KEY` and see the existing name. There is no second preferences key to merge and no new data family to initialize as part of this naming decision. [Persistence envelope](../persistence/persistence-envelope.md), [Format versioning guide](../sharing/format-versioning-guide.md) and [ADR 053](adr-053-docs-in-repo.md) explain the surrounding boundaries.

This preserves the useful local-storage model while making the successor to the old naming decision explicit. Historical context remains in the superseded record; current readers can follow its replacement link here without treating the old pattern as the convention for additional data.

## The current preferences key and value shape

These are the existing declarations. The new naming decision preserves this identifier rather than silently changing where the application reads its preferences.

```ts
export const DEFAULT_SIZE = GRID_SIZES[0];
export const PREFERENCES_KEY = 'neon-pairs.preferences.v1';
export const PREFERENCES_VERSION = 1;
export interface Preferences {
  readonly size: number;
  readonly bestMoves: Readonly<Record<string, number>>;
}
export interface PreferenceStore {
  getItem(key: string): string | null;
  setItem(key: string, value: string): void;
}
```

# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows those cases in detail, and [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runners.

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.
