# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Tournament

Open Tournament beside New Game to run a four- or eight-player knockout on one device. Each match shares one deal; completed attempts are compared by moves, then active time, then seed. Finished brackets are kept in the local Past tournaments list and can be exported or loaded as Tournament JSON. The detailed rules are in [Competition](competition/competition-overview.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

## Documentation map

Every project document, by area. Project-wide policies apply to all new work, including work that doesn't mention them.

### Gameplay

- [rules.md](gameplay/rules.md): Card matching, moves, timing and victory rules
- [deck-generation.md](gameplay/deck-generation.md): Board-code parsing, paired deck construction, deterministic shuffle arithmetic, and fresh seed selection.
- [selection-state.md](gameplay/selection-state.md): The closed, one-card, and mismatch selection alternatives, visibility, and decoding boundaries.
- [turn-resolution.md](gameplay/turn-resolution.md): Activation guards, second-reveal resolution, and the ordering of time, feedback, and turns.
- [scoring-and-moves.md](gameplay/scoring-and-moves.md): Pair progress, move accounting, minimum completions, and continued play at the move cap.
- [best-score-records.md](gameplay/best-score-records.md): Per-size best move comparison, preference validation, persistence, and imported-completion behavior.
- [board-size-catalogue.md](gameplay/board-size-catalogue.md): The seven board sizes, exact card and pair counts, included faces, and size selection behavior.
- [win-conditions.md](gameplay/win-conditions.md): Full matched coverage, the final transition, stopped time, and played versus imported completion.
- [game-state-model.md](gameplay/game-state-model.md): GameState fields, invariants, derived values, immutable transitions, and session boundaries.
- [pair-identity.md](gameplay/pair-identity.md): Position indices versus face numbers, artwork identity dimensions, and hidden-face rendering.
- [mismatch-interval.md](gameplay/mismatch-interval.md): The exact 800-millisecond active interval, synchronization, pauses, and stale timer protection.
- [elapsed-time-rules.md](gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md): Active-time accumulation, browser observations, display conversion, caps, and snapshot precision.

### Controls and input

### Visuals

---
open-forge:
  description: Saved-list retention, aggregate best-score lifetime and the absence
    of an attempt history.
  tags:
    - Persistence
    - Retention
---
# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in [Persistence envelope](persistence-envelope.md). Parsing and validation failures are covered in [Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md), because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. [Best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.

# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. [Persistence overview](persistence-overview.md) describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

[Corrupt data policy](corrupt-data-policy.md) follows the rejection branches in detail. [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. [Storage testing guide](storage-testing-guide.md) extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is [Reproducibility](reproducibility.md). This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See [Format versioning](format-versioning-guide.md) for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in [Board code format](board-code-format.md).

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. [Replay format](replay-format.md) covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See [Reproduction panel](../interface/reproduction-panel.md) and [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. [Snapshot format](snapshot-format.md) gives the complete validation sequence; [Snapshot selection notes](snapshot-selection-notes.md) explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:17:`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:64:New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.
docs/interface/announcements-policy.md:92:The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:48:Tournament history is written when its bracket reaches complete. The preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:52:The app has no account or service that copies either store elsewhere. A best or Tournament history kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies solo game progress; Export tournament copies a Tournament record into the JSON box.
docs/persistence/retention-policy.md:54:The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. Tournament JSON exports one event at a time; it is not a backup of the preference aggregate or the complete saved history.
docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:35:The snapshot textarea has no need for a FormData name in its current path because its value is held in React state and passed directly to `loadSnapshot`. Adding a name attribute alone would not turn its surrounding buttons into a form submission. docs/interface/form-layout-guide.md:93:For a proposed name field, these label and native-control patterns are relevant background, but there is no implemented name form to copy. [Text entry policy](text-entry-policy.md), [Name length policy](name-length-policy.md) and [Duplicate names policy](duplicate-names-policy.md) own its separate acceptance rules. docs/interface/status-bar.md:14:The status bar is a view of the current game and the current size's stored best move count. It does not run the clock, decide matches or write preferences. Keeping these jobs outside the component lets the same output describe ordinary play, a paused import and a completed import without separate counter logic.
docs/interface/status-bar.md:45:Elapsed time starts with the first valid reveal, pauses while the document is hidden or an unfinished imported game awaits Resume, and stops at completion. The game caps it at 359999999ms, whose visible value is `5999:59`. Play can continue at that cap. The status bar has no special disabled state for a maximum clock value.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:21:The reader has no write or removal call. However, `useSavedPreferences` runs an effect on mounting with the preferences obtained during initialization. That effect can overwrite the rejected string with valid fallback preferences after rendering. The original text remains available only until a save occurs, and the ordinary mount effect is such a save.
docs/persistence/corrupt-data-policy.md:107:Invalid input typed into the board-code and snapshot controls follows another interaction. Those controls keep the current game, preserve the draft for correction and show their defined validation status. They do not silently replace the active game with a default board. That feedback is appropriate because the person has just requested an explicit load operation.
docs/interface/name-length-policy.md:13:The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page.
docs/interface/name-length-policy.md:31:In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:3:  description: What the current game saves, what remains in memory and which
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:49:Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.
docs/persistence/persistence-overview.md:69:Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. [Private browsing notes](private-browsing-notes.md) and [Storage quota notes](storage-quota-notes.md) separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:65:A test that fills a different port has not filled the game's origin. A test that navigates away and accidentally starts a different server port may appear to recover simply because it has entered an empty storage area. The artifact server chooses a private port; comparisons across independent runs need to account for that.
docs/persistence/storage-quota-notes.md:73:The current code has no storage estimation call, persistence-permission request or cleanup pass to make room. Its response to a rejected write is to preserve the active session. The app also does not delete another origin user's keys as a recovery measure. [Storage failure policy](storage-failure-policy.md) follows those catches and their visible consequences.
docs/interface/control-bar.md:20:The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.
docs/persistence/_persistence.md:20:- [What the current game saves, what remains in memory and which persistence page to consult.](persistence-overview.md) - #Persistence #Architecture
docs/interface/error-display-guide.md:11:This page explains how failed board-code and snapshot loads are reported without replacing the current game.
docs/persistence/private-browsing-notes.md:28:If the player finishes a game, the current best is updated in memory and may also be written. It can appear again after a same-context reload. When the browser later removes that private context's site data, a new visit has no such value to read. A fresh 4x4 start with no bests is consistent with private-session cleanup.
docs/interface/screen-reader-notes.md:34:Matched cards remain focusable, and navigation does not skip them. During a mismatch or paused import, movement can continue although activating another card has no game effect. This keeps exploration separate from the turn decision. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) traces the remembered tab stop and target calculation.
docs/interface/screen-reader-notes.md:52:A first reveal starts elapsed time but leaves Moves at zero. The game has not yet completed a two-card attempt. It also does not publish a turn result merely for that first card. A user can inspect the newly focused control's name, move to another location and make the second choice.
docs/interface/screen-reader-notes.md:80:Invalid input keeps the current game and draft. The visible outcomes are `Invalid board code.` and `Invalid snapshot.`. The load buttons reference the nearby notice paragraph as a description, and the event feedback path publishes the outcome. Clicking a load button leaves focus there. An invalid Enter submission from Board code leaves focus in the input for correction.
docs/persistence/storage-testing-guide.md:93:For a write-only failure, observe both states: the new best remains in the session, while the browser string is unchanged. A later read gets the earlier persisted state. For a null store, subsequent attempts are no-ops through the captured null rather than fresh browser probes. The current implementation has no retry queue to drain or success flag to wait for.
docs/persistence/storage-testing-guide.md:99:In a writable working checkout, `npm test` runs the unit and static checks. `npm run test:e2e` type checks and builds current source, builds diagnostic entries and then runs browser journeys against the result. The command does not fall back to an older distribution after a failed build.
docs/interface/reproduction-panel.md:18:`Game.tsx` renders Reproduction after the Board. Its native `details` element has class `reproduction` and no `open` attribute, so it starts collapsed. The summary reads `Reproduce a game`, taken from `ReproductionControl.summary` in `control-labels.ts`. Opening and closing the disclosure is browser behavior; the component has no separate expanded-state variable.
docs/interface/reproduction-panel.md:85:A useful manual sequence begins by editing Board code to an invalid value, revealing a card and submitting the draft. The current game remains and the draft survives. Correct it to a valid code, submit with Enter, and inspect the focused Load board button. Export that fresh game, import it, then close the disclosure. The notice and Resume remain available. Navigate on the paused board, resume and observe that focus follows the remembered location.
docs/interface/target-size-policy.md:66:The reproduction summary is another useful case. Its text and disclosure marker occupy only part of a padded native summary element. The element supplies the disclosure interaction. Replacing it with a visually similar small icon could change both target size and semantics; the current source does neither.
docs/interface/target-size-policy.md:84:The current game makes many of these checks straightforward by keeping interaction on native DOM elements. There is no canvas hit-map to reconcile with a drawn target. [Native controls guide](native-controls-guide.md) explains that architectural advantage, while [Contrast audit](../visuals/contrast-audit.md) and [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) cover other properties that a dimension alone cannot establish.
docs/interface/disabled-state-guide.md:32:A player can leave with Tab and return to the remembered matched card. Activating it again has no game effect. This is covered in `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts`, which checks the disabled attribute, continued focus and unchanged move count after another Space activation.
docs/interface/disabled-state-guide.md:62:A player can move focus while paused. Resume returns to the current remembered card before clearing the pause and removing its button. A snapshot with a pending mismatch then continues its remaining interval. A completed import is not paused and has no Resume button; all of its cards are already matched.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:14:The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection.
docs/interface/duplicate-names-policy.md:20:The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name.
docs/interface/native-controls-guide.md:33:Card renders a native button with `type="button"`. Its `onClick` sends an index to the shared activation path. Enter and Space can activate the same control through normal button behavior, so there is no separate keydown implementation of reveal.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:14:The current source contains no dialog component, native dialog element or leave-work handler. New Game, Restart, board-code loading and snapshot loading call the controller directly.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:22:The policy does not define which future feature owns a leave route or a new navigation screen. Those boundaries have to be visible in the feature's actual code. The current page has no router and no alternate play screen. [Focus policy](focus-policy.md) covers orientation when a feature introduces a main-area replacement.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:40:The distinction between cancellation and commitment is observable in game state. Continuing leaves the same deal, revealed selection and counters available. A committed departure may dispose of or replace the session, depending on the feature. The current game has no dialog-specific storage write or serialized marker.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:46:A mismatch stores its remaining active milliseconds in game selection. The session clock advances it when the page is visible and the imported-pause flag is clear. Merely placing a dialog above the board is not one of those conditions in the current source.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:48:Consequently, there is no existing rule here that opening a confirmation pauses the elapsed clock or mismatch. A feature implementation needs to be read for its actual timing behavior rather than assuming that every modal surface freezes play. [Clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) explain the established clock model.
docs/interface/dialog-policy.md:52:The period between opening and making a decision is therefore worth observing in review. It can expose accidental differences between the visual state, current game state and timers. The observation is useful even when the feature's intended behavior is simply to preserve the current clock semantics.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:12:This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.
docs/interface/focus-policy.md:18:`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:14:A useful review follows a few populated journeys and checks source at the transitions. An empty board screenshot cannot show preserved drafts, matched-card focus or a stale timer after Restart. The checks below are grounded in the current source and specifications; links identify the separate policies for feature surfaces that do not exist yet.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:25:The current page has no name editor, dialog or result table. A change introducing one has more scope than styling an existing control. Its relevant policy is linked below, and its current behavior has to be established from its own implementation.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:31:- Grid size is a labeled native select with the seven supported choices, and its selected value agrees with the current game after either successful load type.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:48:- Invalid board-code and snapshot submissions preserve the current game and the entered text, and show their exact existing load outcomes.
docs/interface/interface-review-checklist.md:60:- Unfinished progress loads paused, including an imported position that has not started its clock yet.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:14:Neon Pairs currently asks for a board code and snapshot text, not a player name. There is no name field, group-name store or name rendering component in the source. The name policy below applies when such input is introduced; it does not describe a transformation already applied to the reproduction textarea.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:68:The same is true for error preservation. On malformed JSON, the text remains editable and the current game remains present. That behavior supports correction of a structured draft. Accepted names use the normalized representation described above.
docs/interface/text-entry-policy.md:80:The current game has no name-character allowlist or prohibited-name list. Adding one while implementing spacing cleanup would be a separate product decision, not a consequence of Unicode normalization.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:26:Card has no `onPointerDown`, `onTouchStart`, `onMouseEnter` or context-menu cancellation handler. The game does not reveal the face merely because a pointer enters its bounds. Hover changes a border through CSS. Pointer cancellation has no game action to undo because a press alone did not choose the card.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:54:`.card` sets `touch-action: manipulation`, `user-select: none` and the WebKit-prefixed selection property. The touch-action value retains browser panning and pinch interaction while avoiding a separate application gesture system. The neutral back and face artwork are children of the button; there is no transparent overlay catching touches above them.
docs/interface/pointer-and-touch.md:76:Matched cards retain their full-opacity face and green border when hovered. Clicking one does not add a move. Their continued presence as buttons allows a pointer user to revisit a remembered position and a keyboard user to traverse a consistent grid. [Disabled state guide](disabled-state-guide.md) discusses why semantic unavailability is not implemented as removal from focus order.
docs/sharing/import-safety-policy.md:59:These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.
docs/sharing/sharing-faq.md:57:The browser keeps your current game and the draft you entered. It shows `Invalid board code.` or `Invalid snapshot.` beside the reproduction controls. The active game can continue while you correct the draft; a failed load does not pause it.
docs/sharing/sharing-faq.md:59:Check that you copied the entire JSON object, including closing punctuation, and that the board code has not been altered. A valid JSON object can still describe an invalid game position, such as a single matched card without its partner. The current snapshot notice does not identify the failing field. [Import safety](import-safety-policy.md) describes the validation boundary and diagnostic policy.
docs/sharing/sharing-faq.md:69:Sending text has no effect on the recipient's browser until they load it. A snapshot contains no per-size best records. Loading a completed position displays its result without treating that load as a played winning turn.
docs/sharing/sharing-faq.md:95:The game has no account or trusted result service attached to these artifacts. For a bug report, reproducibility is the useful property: the same code identifies the same deck, and the same valid replay gives the same core transitions.
docs/sharing/reproducibility.md:71:These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:48:Tournament JSON carries a normalized player draft, the tournament's bracket state and an optional current game snapshot. Its exact root keys are `draft`, `format`, `gameSnapshot`, `tournament` and `version`. `Export tournament` fills the Tournament JSON box and `Load tournament` validates the whole object before applying it. The format carries completed move/time results and board codes, but does not certify that those results came from an unedited game.
docs/sharing/data-exchange-policy.md:66:The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.
docs/sharing/replay-format.md:97:The browser may receive a delayed timer callback, but the replay has no scheduler delay. It models the logical rule. Browser synchronization tests separately establish that a click can resolve an overdue mismatch before activation even if a scheduled timer has not run. A successful replay is evidence about core order, while a browser journey is evidence about the adapter's time accounting.
docs/sharing/replay-format.md:169:A new deal begins another replay. The root has one board code and no action that changes size or seed. The format also has no initial snapshot field, so it cannot start halfway through a saved game. To reproduce later behavior, provide earlier actions that produce the desired state, or use a snapshot when only that state is needed.
docs/sharing/snapshot-format.md:31:Root property order has no semantic effect during decoding. The exporter writes `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`, using a two-space indent. Reformatting the JSON does not alter its meaning provided the result stays within the byte limit and preserves the same values.
docs/sharing/snapshot-format.md:56:Loading this object in the browser displays that position paused. Reading it through `decodeSnapshot` alone produces a state whose selection still contains the 300ms interval; the returned `GameState` has no `paused` property. The browser's `replaceGame` creates the pause in its enclosing `Session`. That separation lets the same accepted position be used in a pure test without emulating a Resume control.
docs/sharing/snapshot-format.md:74:`closed` means that there is no revealed unmatched card. It can describe a fresh deal, a state after a matched pair, a state after a miss has closed, or a completed game. Those situations are distinguished by the other fields rather than by extra closed-state labels.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:25:`readMatched` first requires an array. It then creates a new `matched` array and a `Map<number, number>` of counts by face. For each supplied position it checks that the value is a nonnegative safe integer, is below the deck length, and has not already been appended. It reads the generated face, appends the position, and increments that face's count.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:29:The empty array succeeds. The map then has no counts that violate the condition, and the returned empty array is truthy in JavaScript. The outer decoder's `if (!matched)` correctly distinguishes `null` from an accepted empty list. Confusing an empty list with failure in a port would make fresh-state snapshots impossible to load.
docs/sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md:63:A closed selection by itself is not enough to establish a valid snapshot. For example, the outer decoder rejects a closed, started game at zero moves. `readSelection` accepts the shape because it has no responsibility for move history. This small scope makes its failure cases easier to reason about.

--- open-forge: description: Current action focus and board memory, plus the policy for main-screen replacements. tags: - Input - Focus - Policy --- # Focus policy This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen. Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things. ## Existing page and future screens `Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen. A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists. The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. [Dialog policy](dialog-policy.md) covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus. ## Initial load is quiet The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method. The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board. A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing. ## Deal actions retain their location New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call. The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms. A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place. Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. [Error display guide](error-display-guide.md) follows those cases in detail. ## Remembered board focus Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`. Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched. Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. [Board keyboard navigation](board-keyboard-navigation.md) provides the calculations and edge behavior. ## Resume transfers before removal Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target. In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices. The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment. The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location. ## Visible focus and scroll clearance `game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area. The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail. `useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible. The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately. ## Focus is not completion feedback Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched. Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched. These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries. ## Review evidence The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring. A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. [Interface review checklist](interface-review-checklist.md) gathers these journeys with layout and input checks. For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior. --- open-forge: description: Status publication, repeated event identity, turn results and load feedback. tags: - Input - Accessibility - Status --- # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins.
